title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science

Choosing variables
Real world datasets have dozens or hundreds of variables.
How do you choose which ones to include in your model?

Spoiler: “all of them” is not the answer.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Purpose of regression


Inference
Estimate how \(y\) responds to \(x\). You care about the coefficients.
How much does soil Pb decline with each mile from Exide?

Prediction
Estimate \(y\) for new observations. You care about the fitted values.
What’s the soil Pb at a property we haven’t sampled?



In this class (and EDS 241): focus on inference
In EDS 232: focus on prediction

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
If you care about inference
Then you need a strategy for choosing variables to include in, or exclude from, your model.

The wrong choice gives you a biased coefficient, even with infinite data.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Remember Simpson’s paradox?












Leaving out Region reversed the effect of temperature on bleaching.
Region is a confounder. Leaving out a confounder biases your estimated effect.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
The backdoor criterion
More generally, we want to choose variables that satisfy the backdoor criterion.

A backdoor path is a path from \(x\) to \(y\) that starts with an arrow into \(x\).


A set of variables satisfies the backdoor criterion if adjusting for them:

Closes every backdoor path between \(x\) and \(y\), and
Doesn’t include any variables caused by \(x\)



Then the coefficient on \(x\) is an unbiased estimate of its causal effect on \(y\).

Colliders
Why do restaurants in popular locations seem to have worse food?







%%{init: {"themeVariables": {"fontSize": "24px"}}}%%

    f((Food<br/>quality))
    s((Success))

Location and Food quality are independent. Either one can make a restaurant successful.
Location → Success ← Food quality is closed: Success is a collider.

Leave it closed by excluding Success from the model.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Colliders: with and without
























A restaurant can succeed by being in a popular location OR having good food OR both. Adjusting for a collider (success) opens the path and creates a negative relationship between location and food quality that isn’t there.

Distance from Exide affects children’s blood Pb through soil Pb.
There’s no backdoor: no arrows point into Distance.

So it’s not about bias. It’s about which question you’re asking.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Total vs direct effects


Exclude the mediator
The total effect of distance: everything that changes when you move farther from Exide.

Include the mediator
The direct effect of distance: what changes when you move farther but hold soil Pb constant.



Here the direct effect is ~0. Distance only matters because of soil Pb. Neither model is biased, they answer different questions!

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Recap

Confounders open backdoor paths that must be blocked. Include them.
Colliders close paths. Leave them alone. Exclude them.
Mediators need careful thought. Include them for the direct effect, exclude them for the total effect.

Simulate causes before effects. Follow the arrows!

set.seed(1)
n <- 300
confound <- tibble(
  farm_size = rnorm(n, mean = 100, sd = 30),
  pesticide = rnorm(n, mean = 2 + 0.05 * farm_size, sd = 1),
  bees = rnorm(n, mean = 60 - 3 * pesticide - 0.2 * farm_size, sd = 5)
)

confound_adj_lm <- lm(bees ~ pesticide + farm_size, confound)

Goal: choose variables for your model that avoid bias.


Before you write any code, make a DAG that describes what you think the causal relationships are

Close the open ones (confounders) and leave the closed ones alone (colliders)
Decide whether you want the total or direct effect (mediators)

title: Lab 2: Investigating claims using inference
text:
Investigating “yes/no” questions with permutation
Let’s investigate the claim “Lead is elevated in the drip line compared to the rest of the yard” as a yes/no question.

State your hypotheses
Recall that it is more straightforward to find evidence against a hypothesis than for it. So when we investigate yes/no questions, we set up a null hypothesis and see how much evidence there is against it.
State the null and alternative hypotheses for this claim.
\(H_0\):
\(H_A\):


Calculate the observed value of the statistic
We’ll use the difference in means between samples from the drip line and the yard as the statistic for this question.






Important



Remember, the mean isn’t always the most appropriate statistic for representing a distribution! Always think critically about how your data relates to the question.


Calculate the difference in means between the drip line and yard observations in the sample. Remember, this should be a single number (not a data frame or pair of means).


Shuffle the predictor variable and recalculate the statistic
This statistical experiment simulates the expected variation in our statistic (difference in means) just due to chance alone. To conduct this experiment, we have to break the connection between the predictor variable (location code) and response (lead concentration). Randomizing the predictor leaves the variation in the response untouched, while removing any assocation between the two.
Shuffle the predictor variable and recalculate the statistic. Do it just once - we’ll repeat in the next section.






Tip



sample() can be used to shuffle vectors.




Repeat shuffling
In the previous section, you simulated one statistic from the null hypothesis. What we need now is a whole bunch of statistics from the null hypothesis - our null distribution.
Repeat shuffling 10,000 times to create a vector that simulates the null distribution.






Tip



replicate() repeatedly runs expressions over and over.


Visualize the null distribution using a histogram.


Compare the observed to the null
The previous figure showed the expected distribution of the statistic (the difference in mean lead between drip line and yard) under the null hypothesis. How does that compare to the observed value?
Plot the null distribution again, but this time add a vertical line indicating the observed statistic.
Calculate your p-value.






Note



A p-value is the probability of observing the sample (or something more extreme) if the null hypothesis is true.




Interpret your results
Based on your p-value, do you reject or fail to reject the null hypothesis?
What does this mean for your question?
What characteristics of the data may impact your inference?

title: Lab 2: Investigating claims using inference
text:
Investigating “how much?” questions with bootstrapping
Now, let’s investigate the claim “Neighborhoods north of the Exide plant were exposed to more lead than those south” as a how much? question.

Calculate the observed value of the statistic
Once again, let’s use the difference in means as our statistic. Calculate the difference in means between properties in the extended north area and those in the extended south area.






Tip



Use dplyr functions to wrangle the soil core data for this part. Properties starting with “ENA” are in the extended north area, and the “ESA” prefix means extended south area. str_sub() will help here.




Resample observations and recalculate the statistic
Bootstrapping simulates the expected variation in our statistic (difference in means) from sampling. Compare this to permutation, which is about variation just due to chance. For this experiment, we will assume the sample is representative of the population and repeatedly draw “new” samples. This process simulates the process of collecting new samples.
Resample rows from the data frame and recalculate the statistic. Repeat this 10,000 times to simulate the sampling distribution.






Tip



Use slice_sample() with replacement to get bootstrap samples.


Visualize the sampling distribution using a histogram.


Find the confidence interval
The previous figure showed how your statistic varies due to slight differences between samples. Use this sampling distribution to estimate the 95% confidence interval.






Note



A confidence interval is a range of values that you are confident contains the population parameter.








Tip



Use the quantile() function to find the middle 95% of the sampling distribution.


Plot the sampling distribution again, but this time add vertical lines indicating the observed statistic and the 95% CI.


Interpret your results
Based on your confidence interval, how much could the difference in lead exposure between north and south be?
What does this mean for your question?
What characteristics of the data may impact your inference?

Is the categorical variable useful?
Coefficients describe relationships between levels - but is the categorical variable as a whole useful?

Frame this question as:

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
section: Degrees of freedom are inference currency
text:
Degrees of freedom are inference currency
Data give us information: \(n\) observations
Parameters spend that information: \(p\) coefficients
What’s left over is our degrees of freedom
\[
df = n - p
\]

Leftover df are what we use to estimate the noise, \(\sigma\). Fewer df, less certain \(\hat \sigma\), wider CIs, bigger p-values.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
The information-complexity trade off
More parameters spend \(df\) to improve fit.

Too few parameters: the model misses real structure (underfitting)
Too many parameters: the model fits the noise (overfitting)


Every parameter has to earn its df.

text:

Rural, suburban, and urban frogs: svl ~ 1
\[

\epsilon &\sim Normal(0, \sigma)
\end{align}
\]



\(n\) = 104 frogs
\(p\) = 1 coefficient (\(\beta_0\))
\(df\) = 104 - 1 = 103

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
section: Quantify the trade off: the F statistic
text:
Quantify the trade off: the F statistic
\[
F = \frac{(RSS_{simple} - RSS_{complex}) \ / \ (p_{complex} - p_{simple})}{RSS_{complex} \ / \ (n - p_{complex})}
\]

Numerator: improvement in fit per df spent
Denominator: leftover noise per df remaining


If the extra parameters only fit noise, \(F \approx 1\). Bigger \(F\) means the extra parameters were worth it.

section: Where does the p-value come from?
text:
Where does the p-value come from?
If \(H_0\) is true (all habitat means are equal), \(F\) follows an F distribution with \((p_{complex} - p_{simple}, \ n - p_{complex})\) df.

Only the right tail counts: extra parameters can only reduce RSS.

text:
Interpret the ANOVA
\(H_0\): \(\mu_{rural} = \mu_{suburban} = \mu_{urban}\)
\(H_A\): at least one habitat mean differs

If habitat had no relationship with size, we’d see an F at least this large in 10.2% of samples. Fail to reject \(H_0\).


But we pooled frogs of all ages, and frogs keep growing as they age. Age differences are hiding in the residuals, inflating the denominator of \(F\). Could accounting for age change the answer? You’ll find out in lab.

text:

More data means more information (df) to spend on inference.
What do we spend it on? Parameters.
More complex models explain more variation, but do they explain enough variation to justify their costs? The F statistic answers that.

ANOVA isn’t a separate tool from linear models. It’s a comparison between two linear models.

title: Lab 1: Reliability of Soil Lead Measurements
text:
Between November 2013 and July 2015, contractors working under the oversight of the California Department of Toxic Substances Control (DTSC) sampled soil lead concentrations at hundreds of residential properties near the former Exide Technologies battery recycling facility in Vernon, CA. Crews collected soil cores from several locations on each property and analyzed them in a laboratory for lead content. This sampling campaign, and this lab’s data, are described in the DTSC Preliminary Estimate of the Geographical Boundary of Emissions report (Department of Toxic Substances Control 2015).
A single soil sample is a measurement of a property’s soil lead level, but no single measurement perfectly captures the “true” lead burden of an entire property. In this lab you’ll explore how much soil lead measurements vary within a property, and how that variability depends on where on the property a sample was taken. This is a question about reliability: if you sampled the same property twice, how close would the two measurements be?

title: Lab 1: Reliability of Soil Lead Measurements
text:
The data
exide-soil-cores.csv contains a subset of the DTSC’s public data table for the Exide site. You can find it on Workbench under /courses/EDS222/data. It’s limited to the samples collected during the initial and expanded assessments in 2013-2015. The full DTSC public data table contains lots more - you are encouraged to explore it further!

Data dictionary







Column
Description




property_id
Identifier for the property a sample was collected from.


sample_id
Identifier for an individual soil sample (boring).


sample_date
Date the sample was collected.


location_code
Where on the property the sample was taken. DL = drip line. YD = yard.


pb_ppm
Lead concentration, in parts per million (ppm).


longitude, latitude
Coordinates of the property (WGS84).





What does a row represent?
Each row is one soil core collected from one location on one property, at a depth of 3 inches below ground surface. Properties were sampled at multiple locations, so property_id repeats across rows: a single property typically contributes up to ten yard samples and a handful of drip line samples.


What’s a drip line?
The drip line is the narrow strip of soil at the edge of a building’s roof - the line where rainwater drips or is directed off the roof and gutters. It sits right against the house, in contrast to the rest of the yard, the more open part of the property further from the building. Because paint (a historical source of lead) tends to chip and weather off exterior walls, and because roof runoff concentrates atmospheric deposition falling on the roof into a narrow band, drip line soil can experience different pollutant exposure than yard soil.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Empirical and parametric samples
Empirical: derived directly from observations
Parametric: derived from a mathematical formula governed by one or a few parameters

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Empirical samples: random
The process of collecting real observations is how we get empirical samples.
When feasible, simple random samples are most representative of the population.

IMS Figure 2.1: a simple random sample of recent graduates.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Empirical samples: biased
A truly random sample is rarely possible. Without care, there are many ways for biases to creep in. Convenience bias is particularly common.

IMS Figure 2.2: a biased sample.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Empirical samples: stratified
Even if simple random sampling is infeasible, sampling strategies reduce bias. For example, stratified sampling divides the population into self-similar groups, then randomly samples within those groups.


IMS Figure 2.4: a stratified sample.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Example of a parametric distribution

Parametric distributions are defined by parameters (instead of observed data).

E.g., a normal distribution has two parameters - the mean controls location and the sd controls shape.

Recall probability density functions (PDFs) tell us how probable different ranges of values are.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Parameterizing a distribution
Let’s parameterize a normal distribution with the mean and sd of the lead soil dataset.

soil_cores |>
  summarize(
    mean_pb_ppm = mean(pb_ppm),
    sd_pb_ppm = sd(pb_ppm)
  )

  mean_pb_ppm sd_pb_ppm
        <dbl>     <dbl>
1        253.      371.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Probability density function

The PDF describes the relative probability of observing different values.
This PDF is a normal distribution with parameters matching the lead soil dataset.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
A universe of parametric distributions

The normal distribution is a poor stand-in for the lead data (symmetric, possibly negative).
A different family (e.g. the lognormal) could do a better job. We’ll cover these more in later weeks.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Sampling parametric distributions

We will sample from parametric distributions frequently in this course.
Think of the height of the PDF as the chance of observing a nearby value.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Empirical and parametric samples
Empirical: derived directly from observations.

E.g., lead concentrations in soil cores.

Parametric: derived from a mathematical formula governed by one or a few parameters.

E.g., a normal distribution with a mean and sd.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Sampling strategies

Simple random is most representative of the population, but often infeasible.
Sampling bias misleads inferences about the population.
Sampling strategies (e.g. stratification) work around biases.


IMS Figure 2.1: a simple random sample of recent graduates.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Parametric distributions

Parametric distributions are mathematical functions governed by parameters.
We use them as theoretical stand-ins for populations.
PDF says how probable observations are, given parameters.

Learning objectives

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
section: Statistics is part of the scientific method
text:
Statistics is part of the scientific method

Ask a question
Formulate a (scientific) hypothesis
Conduct a study, experimental or observational
Analyze data
Interpret and communicate the results

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
section: Statistics is part of the scientific method
text:
Statistics is part of the scientific method

Where did lead from the Exide plant end up?
Wind carried more lead NE than SW.
Gather soil cores to measure lead concentrations across the region.
STATS STATS STATS
Interpret and communicate the results

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Two types of hypotheses


What a scientist means
Hypothesis: a testable, causal explanation for an observation

Lead emissions spread via wind.


What a statistician means
Hypothesis: a quantitative statement about a parameter of the population

The proportion of homes downwind of the plant with elevated lead levels is greater than those upwind.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Variation is natural
A statistician knows that a difference in a sample (between proportions, means, etc) is insufficient to evaluate a hypothesis.
Sampling is random!
The real question: is the difference bigger than we’d expect from sampling? Or is it consistent with sampling variation?

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text: Variation is natural

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Assess the evidence
Given that variation is natural in sampling, how do we assess evidence?
We can’t gather new data, so we design statistical experiments based on the sample we have.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
section: Permutation is a statistical experiment for yes/no questions
text:
Permutation is a statistical experiment for yes/no questions
Question: Is the proportion of high risk homes higher downwind than upwind?
Let’s reframe this as:
Question: If there was no relationship between lead risk and wind direction, then how often would our sample be observed?

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Random to the rescue
We can simulate the “what if there’s no relationship?” scenario by randomizing the predictor variable.
Randomization breaks the link between predictor and response, but keeps all the variation from the sample.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Procedure
\(H_0\): there is no relationship/effect/etc
\(H_A\): there is a relationship/effect/etc

Calculate the observed value of the statistic (e.g., a difference in proportions)
Shuffle the predictor variable and recalculate the statistic.
Repeat step 2 until the cows come home (null distribution of the statistic)
Compare the observed value to the null statistic (p-value)
Reject, or fail to reject, the null hypothesis

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text: Permutation visualized

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
section: Compare the observed to the null statistic
text: Compare the observed to the null statistic

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Interpret the p-value
A p-value is the probability of seeing the observed sample, if the null hypothesis is true. That’s it.
If p is less than some threshold (often 0.05 by default), then we say there is a statistically significant result. This means the sample is improbable under chance alone.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Don’t misinterpret the p-value
The following are common misconceptions:

A p-value is the probability that the null hypothesis is true
A statistically significant result is meaningful by real-world standards
A statistically non-significant result means there’s no effect

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Permutation recap

Given only one sample, how do we estimate the natural variation of the statistic? With randomization!
Permutation breaks the connection between the predictor and response, simulating the variation of the statistic expected by chance.
Permutation yields a p-value, which says if your result is statistically significant.

You are wise enough to hold complexity.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
section: Bootstrapping is a statistical experiment for “how much?” questions
text:
Bootstrapping is a statistical experiment for “how much?” questions
Question: How much higher is the proportion of high risk homes downwind than upwind?
Let’s reframe this as:
Question: What’s the interval that we confidently think contains the population-level parameter?

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Random to the rescue

We can simulate the variation in our statistic by resampling the observations.
We’re making the critical assumption that our sample is representative of the population

Instead of getting new samples from the population (too hard!) we get “bootstrapped” samples from the sample itself.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Procedure

Calculate the observed value of the statistic (e.g., a difference in proportions)
Resample the observations with replacement and recalculate the statistic.
Repeat step 2 until the cows come home (sampling distribution)
Find the range containing a large percentage of the sampling distribution (confidence interval)

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text: Bootstrapping visualized

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text: Find your confidence interval

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Interpret your confidence interval
A confidence interval is a range of values that you are confident contains the population parameter.
But wait… what exactly are we confident in?
If we repeated this procedure 100 times, about 95 of those CIs would contain the population parameter.
Our confidence is in the procedure’s long-run accuracy.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Don’t misinterpret your confidence interval
The following are common misconceptions:

There’s a 95% chance the 95% CI contains the population parameter
Larger sample sizes yield more accurate confidence intervals

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Bootstrapping recap

Given only one sample, how do we estimate the natural variation of the statistic? With randomization!
Bootstrapping draws “new” samples from the original, simulating the variation of the statistic expected by sampling.
Bootstrapping yields a confidence interval, which describes a range the actual parameter probably falls in.

CIs rigorously communicate uncertainty.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Permutation vs bootstrapping


Permutation simulates a scenario with no relationship to answer “yes/no” questions.










Bootstrapping simulates the original scenario to answer “how much?” questions.

title: Lab 4: Simulate Simpson’s Paradox
text:
Simulate the data
You’ve chosen your parameters (\(\beta\)s and \(\sigma\)). Define them here:

# These values chosen to represent a scenario where typing faster increases
# typos, but faster typists on average commit fewer typos. If you ignore the
# second predictor (who is typing) then an apparent negative relationship
# emerges, suggesting typing faster reduces typos.
beta_0 <- 10 # Intercept
beta_1 <- 0.1 # Additional typos per increase in speed
beta_2 <- -10 # Difference between typist B and the reference level (typist A)
sigma <- 3 # Standard deviation of the residuals


Generate random values

Simulate your predictor variables. Remember, for Simpson’s paradox to emerge, there has to be a dependency between the two predictor variables.


# Sample size
N <- 50
# Typist identities
typist <- sample(c("A", "B"), N, replace = TRUE)
# Dummy variable for typist B
typistB <- ifelse(typist == "B", 1, 0)
# Typing speed is _greater_ for typist B, who is also less error-prone
typing_speed <- rnorm(N, mean = ifelse(typist == "B", 100, 45), sd = 15)


Calculate the expected value of the response. This is similar to regression with a single predictor, but includes a second term.

\[
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2
\]

expected_typos <- beta_0 + beta_1 * typing_speed + beta_2 * typistB


Simulate the response variable. This is the same as regression with a single predictor. The expected value incorporates the influence of the multiple predictors. Once you have that number, you just need normally-distributed residuals.


typos <- rnorm(
  n = N,
  mean = expected_typos,
  sd = sigma
)

Visualize your simulated data. Verify it’s comparable to your original drawing. If necessary, tweak your parameter values until it represents your scenario reasonably well.

simulated_typing <- tibble(typing_speed, typos, typist)

ggplot(simulated_typing, aes(x = typing_speed, y = typos, fill = typist)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, shape = 21) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("peachpuff", "lightskyblue1"))

speed_typist <- lm(typos ~ typing_speed + typist, data = simulated_typing)

title: Lab 5: Concept maps
section: A guide to making useful concept maps
text:
A guide to making useful concept maps
There are three levels of usefulness, each building on the previous one. Aim to reach the third level!

Level one: concept list
This is the result of your brainstorm: a list of keywords and concepts for the week. It’s an essential first step, and the raw material for building something more useful.


Level two: hierarchical concepts
Arrange your concepts hierarchically, so core concepts are in the middle and supporting concepts branch off of them. Connect related concepts with lines. This structure shows both priority and relationships. But don’t stop here!


Level three: linking words
This is the easiest step to skip, but it’s the most important. Linking words turn undefined connections into a useful mental model. This is how you internalize the relationships between, for example, standard deviation, standard error, and \(\sigma\).



A concept map about concept maps, exhibiting hierarchical concepts related by linking words

title: Lab 5: Concept maps
text:
Instructions

Find your group members (e.g., Week 1 Monday) and your counterparts (e.g., Week 1 Wednesday).
Share your keywords with each other and create a combined list. Revise your combined list by adding, editing, or removing terms where helpful. Write each concept on a sticky note. Now you’ve reached level one: a concept list.
As a group, arrange your concepts hierarchically. Identify the most important concepts and the supporting concepts related to them. Move the sticky notes around to reflect the hierarchy. Once you’re all happy with the configuration, make a digital version. You can use presentation software (e.g., Google Slides), diagramming tools (e.g., Lucid), or sketching/notetaking apps. Now you’ve reached level two: hierarchical concepts.
Give each link between concepts one or more linking words. Examples include “leads to”, “depends on”, “is a type of”, and “produces”. This is the tricky part, and you’ll likely need to rearrange your concepts as you go. Now you’ve reached level three: linking words.
Export your digital concept map to an image or PDF and add it to this shared presentation.

title: Lab 5: Concept maps
text:
Tips

The goal of a concept map is to see the forest for the trees. Now is not the time for in-the-weeds detail. Your map should be a visual explanation of how the tools in your toolbox are related.
You know your linking words work if the two concepts and their link read as a complete thought (e.g., “Lead paint flakes into soil lead”).
There’s no such thing as a “perfect” or “correct” concept map. A concept map is useful if it helps turn individual pieces of knowledge into a more cohesive whole.

title: Week 1 Wednesday pre-class
text:
Example
Describe the claim
Corals growing near islands with healthy seabird colonies grow more than twice as fast as corals near islands where invasive rats have wiped out the seabirds.
Where did you find it?
Audubon Magazine The Remarkable Healing Power of Seabird Poop for Climate-Stressed Coral Reefs
What challenge of statistics does it fall under?
Generalize from treatment to control. The “treatment” is the presence of invasive rats (which extirpate seabirds), the “control” is islands without rats.
Pick the most salient variable in the data. In what ways does it accurately represent what its meant to, and in what ways might it be different? (I.e., assess its validity.)
Coral growth rate. This was measured using the area of corals from photographs1. The claim about growth rate is really more about mass or volume, however area is a reasonably valid proxy because previous research has established area and mass are highly correlated.
Continuing with the same variable, what are the limitations on its reliability?
Estimates of area from photographs are sensitive to the angle of the photo and the judgement of the researcher who traces the photo. Although those factors can affect reliability, the study used photos from divers, which are more reliable than photos taken by aircraft or satellites.
Continuing with the same variable, how was the sample collected? Were there obstacles to selecting a representative sample?
The sample came from twelve islands in the Chagos Archipelago (six had rats, six didn’t). There is potential selection bias because this was an observational study, so the researchers couldn’t randomize which islands got rats and which didn’t. Also, the study only looked at one species of coral. It’s possible other corals are more or less affected by seabird abundance.

text:
Course Description
Statistics is the science of collecting, manipulating, and analyzing empirical data. In this class, we will learn the statistical fundamentals that will enable us to draw conclusions about the environment and its interaction with social and economic systems. We will cover fundamental statistical concepts and tools, and then apply and expand upon those tools to learn some temporal and spatial statistical methods that are particularly helpful in environmental data science. Welcome!

Learning objectives
The goal of this course is to enable MEDS students to confidently and competently apply statistical tools to socio-environmental datasets. Essential skills and concepts are:

Summarize data numerically and graphically
Interpret random variables
Simulate data to test assumptions
Describe models using statistical notation
Draw DAGs to clarify causal relationships
Quantify uncertainty to perform inference

Conditions when mathematical models work well
Two conditions are required for the mathematical model approach to work well:

Independence
Sample size

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Independence

Data are independent when observations don’t influence each other.
Controlled experiments are designed to produce independent observations. In observational studies, complete independence is rare.
Common sources of dependence include:

Geographic or temporal proximity
Repeated measures from the same entity
Shared ancestry or social group

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Sample size

The normal approximation fails more often for very small samples
As a guideline, each group in the sample should have at least 10 expected successes and failures
\(p_1 n_1\), \((1 - p_1) n_1\), \(p_2 n_2\), and \((1 - p_2) n_2\) all \(\ge 10\)
When proportions are close to 0 or 1, this condition gets harder to meet

Interpretations


\(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\), \(H_A: \beta_1 \ne 0\). The p-value is 0.024.
If farmland had no effect on nitrate, a slope at least as far from 0 as 0.037 would be unlikely (p < 0.05). Reject \(H_0\).
We are 95% confident that nitrate increases by between 0.005 and 0.069 mg/L for each additional percentage point of farmland.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
True or false?


The p-value is the probability that \(H_0\) is true.

False. It’s the probability of a statistic at least this extreme if \(H_0\) were true.

If we repeated the study many times, about 95% of our 95% confidence intervals would contain \(\beta_1\).

True. “95% confident” describes the method, not this one interval.

A small p-value means farmland causes higher nitrate.

False. That’s what the rest of today is about.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Precise \(\ne\) unbiased
A small p-value and a narrow confidence interval mean \(\hat \beta_1\) is precise.
They don’t mean it’s unbiased.

If our model leaves out a confounder, or includes a collider, then \(\hat \beta_1\) is precisely estimating the wrong thing. More data makes the interval narrower around the wrong value.


Which variables belong in the model? Back to DAGs.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
DAG vocabulary
Directed Acyclic Graph: your theory of what causes what.

Nodes: variables (measured or not!)
Arrows: direct causal effects
Path: any route from \(x\) to \(y\) along arrows
Causal path: every arrow points toward \(y\)
Backdoor path: starts with an arrow into \(x\)

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Open and closed paths
A path is open if association can flow along it. Each variable on a path either passes it along or blocks it.

Open

Closed

Colliders are the odd one out: adjusting for them opens a path.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
The backdoor criterion
A set of variables satisfies the backdoor criterion if adjusting for them:

Closes every backdoor path between \(x\) and \(y\), and
Doesn’t include any variables caused by \(x\)


Then the coefficient on \(x\) is an unbiased estimate of its causal effect on \(y\).

title: Lab 1: Reliability of Soil Lead Measurements
text:
Between November 2013 and July 2015, contractors working under the oversight of the California Department of Toxic Substances Control (DTSC) sampled soil lead concentrations at hundreds of residential properties near the former Exide Technologies battery recycling facility in Vernon, CA. Crews collected soil cores from several locations on each property and analyzed them in a laboratory for lead content. This sampling campaign, and this lab’s data, are described in the DTSC Preliminary Estimate of the Geographical Boundary of Emissions report (Department of Toxic Substances Control 2015).
A single soil sample is a measurement of a property’s soil lead level, but no single measurement perfectly captures the “true” lead burden of an entire property. In this lab you’ll explore how much soil lead measurements vary within a property, and how that variability depends on where on the property a sample was taken. This is a question about reliability: if you sampled the same property twice, how close would the two measurements be?

title: Lab 1: Reliability of Soil Lead Measurements
text:
The data
exide-soil-cores.csv contains a subset of the DTSC’s public data table for the Exide site. You can find it on Workbench under /courses/EDS222/data. It’s limited to the samples collected during the initial and expanded assessments in 2013-2015. The full DTSC public data table contains lots more - you are encouraged to explore it further!

Data dictionary







Column
Description




property_id
Identifier for the property a sample was collected from.


sample_id
Identifier for an individual soil sample (boring).


sample_date
Date the sample was collected.


location_code
Where on the property the sample was taken. DL = drip line. YD = yard.


pb_ppm
Lead concentration, in parts per million (ppm).


longitude, latitude
Coordinates of the property (WGS84).





What does a row represent?
Each row is one soil core collected from one location on one property, at a depth of 3 inches below ground surface. Properties were sampled at multiple locations, so property_id repeats across rows: a single property typically contributes up to ten yard samples and a handful of drip line samples.


What’s a drip line?
The drip line is the narrow strip of soil at the edge of a building’s roof - the line where rainwater drips or is directed off the roof and gutters. It sits right against the house, in contrast to the rest of the yard, the more open part of the property further from the building. Because paint (a historical source of lead) tends to chip and weather off exterior walls, and because roof runoff concentrates atmospheric deposition falling on the roof into a narrow band, drip line soil can experience different pollutant exposure than yard soil.

title: Lab 6: Urban toads
text:
Cities build stormwater ponds to manage runoff, and amphibians breed in them. Are these ponds good habitat? If urban habitat is lower quality, urban amphibians should grow more slowly and be smaller at the same age than rural amphibians. Smaller females lay fewer eggs, so size matters for population persistence.
Jennette et al. (2019) measured female American toads (Anaxyrus americanus) breeding in rural, suburban, and urban ponds in Baltimore County, Maryland.

habitat: rural, suburban, or urban
svl: snout-vent length (mm), a measure of body size
weight: somatic dry weight
age: years, estimated from growth rings in toe bones (skeletochronology)

In the pre-class slides, you compared the sizes of wood frogs among habitats. Today you’ll ask the same question for toads, then ask one more: does habitat matter once we account for age? Each question is a comparison between a simpler and a more complex model.

title: Lab 6: Urban toads
text:
Cities build stormwater ponds to manage runoff, and amphibians breed in them. Are these ponds good habitat? If urban habitat is lower quality, urban amphibians should grow more slowly and be smaller at the same age than rural amphibians. Smaller females lay fewer eggs, so size matters for population persistence.
Jennette et al. (2019) measured female American toads (Anaxyrus americanus) breeding in rural, suburban, and urban ponds in Baltimore County, Maryland.

habitat: rural, suburban, or urban
svl: snout-vent length (mm), a measure of body size
weight: somatic dry weight
age: years, estimated from growth rings in toe bones (skeletochronology)

In the pre-class slides, you compared the sizes of wood frogs among habitats. Today you’ll ask the same question for toads, then ask one more: does habitat matter once we account for age? Each question is a comparison between a simpler and a more complex model.

toads <- read_csv("../data/female-american-toads.csv") |>
  mutate(
    habitat = str_to_title(POP) # Convert to title case
  ) |>
  select(habitat, svl = SVL, weight = Weight, age = Age)

title: Lab 6: Urban toads
text:
Part 1: Explore
Make a plot of toad size (SVL) by habitat.

ggplot(toads, aes(habitat, svl)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "SVL (mm)")








How many toads are in each habitat? Which habitat is the reference level?

count(toads, habitat)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  habitat      n
  <chr>    <int>
1 Rural       50
2 Suburban    24
3 Urban       30

sort(unique(toads$habitat))

[1] "Rural"    "Suburban" "Urban"   


Answer: 50 rural, 24 suburban, and 30 urban toads. Rural is the reference level. habitat is text, so lm() sorts its values alphabetically and uses the first one as the reference.

title: Lab 6: Urban toads
text:
Part 2: One-way ANOVA

State the hypotheses
Question: Does toad size differ among habitats?
\(H_0\): \(\mu_{rural} = \mu_{suburban} = \mu_{urban}\)
\(H_A\): at least one habitat mean differs


Fit the models
Fit the simpler model (intercept-only) and the more complex model (habitat).

null_lm <- lm(svl ~ 1, toads)
habitat_lm <- lm(svl ~ habitat, toads)
summary(habitat_lm)


Call:
lm(formula = svl ~ habitat, data = toads)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-12.7933  -3.7558  -0.6318   3.7750  15.1967 

Coefficients:
                Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)      81.2800     0.8239  98.652   <2e-16 ***
habitatSuburban  -2.6767     1.4467  -1.850   0.0672 .  
habitatUrban     -2.2663     1.3454  -1.684   0.0952 .  
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 5.826 on 101 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.04404,   Adjusted R-squared:  0.02511 
F-statistic: 2.326 on 2 and 101 DF,  p-value: 0.1029


Interpret each coefficient of habitat_lm in a sentence.
Answer: Rural toads average 81.3 mm SVL (\(\hat\beta_0\)). Suburban toads average 2.7 mm smaller than rural toads (\(\hat\beta_1\)), and urban toads average 2.3 mm smaller than rural toads (\(\hat\beta_2\)).


Calculate F by hand
Recall the F statistic:
\[
F = \frac{(RSS_{simple} - RSS_{complex}) \ / \ (p_{complex} - p_{simple})}{RSS_{complex} \ / \ (n - p_{complex})}
\]

\(RSS\): residual sum of squares, \(\sum (y_i - \hat y_i)^2\). The variation the model leaves unexplained.
\(p\): number of coefficients the model estimates, including the intercept
\(n\): number of observations

Calculate each piece, then F.

rss_simple <- sum(residuals(null_lm)^2)
rss_complex <- sum(residuals(habitat_lm)^2)
p_simple <- length(coef(null_lm))
p_complex <- length(coef(habitat_lm))
n <- nrow(toads)

f_stat <- ((rss_simple - rss_complex) / (p_complex - p_simple)) /
  (rss_complex / (n - p_complex))
f_stat

[1] 2.326308




Check your work
Compare your F statistic to R’s.

anova(null_lm, habitat_lm)

Analysis of Variance Table

Model 1: svl ~ 1
Model 2: svl ~ habitat
  Res.Df  RSS Df Sum of Sq      F Pr(>F)
1    103 3586                           
2    101 3428  2    157.91 2.3263 0.1029




Interpret
What do you conclude? Use the p-value in your answer.
Answer: If toad size didn’t differ among habitats, we’d see an F statistic at least this large about 10% of the time (p = 0.10). We fail to reject \(H_0\). Spending 2 df on habitat didn’t buy enough reduction in RSS.

title: Lab 6: Urban toads
text:
Part 3: Account for age

What’s hiding in the residuals?
Toads keep growing after they mature. Plot SVL against age, colored by habitat.

ggplot(toads, aes(age, svl, color = habitat)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "SVL (mm)", color = NULL)








What fraction of the variation in SVL does age explain on its own? Compare to habitat.

age_lm <- lm(svl ~ age, toads)
summary(age_lm)$r.squared

[1] 0.3188451

summary(habitat_lm)$r.squared

[1] 0.04403692


Answer: Age explains 32% of the variation in SVL. Habitat explains only 4%.


Why does that matter for our F-test?
Look at the denominator of F. In the one-way ANOVA, the variation due to age is stuck in the residuals.
Explain in your own words how leaving age out of the model affects the F statistic for habitat.
Answer: Variation due to age inflates \(RSS_{complex}\), the denominator of F. A noisier denominator makes the same difference among habitats look smaller relative to the noise. Accounting for age shrinks the denominator, so differences among habitats are easier to detect.


Compare models
Question: Does habitat explain enough variation to justify its cost, after accounting for age?
Fit the additive model. Compare it to the age-only model.

additive_lm <- lm(svl ~ age + habitat, toads)
anova(age_lm, additive_lm)

Analysis of Variance Table

Model 1: svl ~ age
Model 2: svl ~ age + habitat
  Res.Df    RSS Df Sum of Sq      F  Pr(>F)  
1    102 2442.6                              
2    100 2241.2  2    201.33 4.4915 0.01355 *
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1




Interpret
What do you conclude? Use the p-value in your answer.
Answer: If habitat had no relationship with size among toads of the same age, we’d see an F statistic at least this large about 1% of the time (p = 0.014). We reject \(H_0\). After accounting for age, habitat explains enough variation to justify spending 2 df.
Interpret the urban coefficient in a sentence.

summary(additive_lm)


Call:
lm(formula = svl ~ age + habitat, data = toads)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-10.722  -3.305  -0.405   2.898  13.162 

Coefficients:
                Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)      64.0025     2.4669  25.944  < 2e-16 ***
age               3.7560     0.5162   7.277 7.87e-11 ***
habitatSuburban  -2.1446     1.1779  -1.821   0.0716 .  
habitatUrban     -3.1427     1.0999  -2.857   0.0052 ** 
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 4.734 on 100 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.375, Adjusted R-squared:  0.3562 
F-statistic:    20 on 3 and 100 DF,  p-value: 3.115e-10


Answer: Urban toads are 3.1 mm smaller than rural toads of the same age.

title: Lab 6: Urban toads
text:
Part 4: Check assumptions
Linear models assume the residuals have constant variance. Check the additive model: the spread of residuals should be similar across habitats.

toads |>
  mutate(residual = residuals(additive_lm)) |>
  ggplot(aes(habitat, residual)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Residual (mm)")








Are the assumptions reasonable?
Answer: Yes. The residual spread is similar across habitats.

title: Lab 6: Urban toads
text:
Part 5: Statistical vs biological significance
The urban coefficient is statistically significant. Is it biologically meaningful? Express the urban effect as a percentage of average rural size, and compare it to the growth from one extra year of age.

coef(additive_lm)[["habitatUrban"]] /
  mean(toads$svl[toads$habitat == "Rural"])

[1] -0.03866546

coef(additive_lm)[["habitatUrban"]] / coef(additive_lm)[["age"]]

[1] -0.836727


Answer: Urban toads are about 4% smaller than rural toads. That’s roughly 0.8 years of growth: an urban toad is about the size of a rural toad almost a year younger. Because female size drives egg production, that gap could reduce reproductive output in urban habitats.
Jennette et al. found no difference in the ages of breeding adults among habitats, but urban toads were smaller at every age. Which life stage does that point to as the problem in urban habitats: adults, or larvae and juveniles? Why?
Answer: Larvae and juveniles. If urban adult habitat were worse, urban toads would start adulthood at a similar size and fall further behind as they age. Instead, Jennette et al. found the size gap was similar across ages, so urban toads start adulthood smaller. That points to the stormwater ponds or juvenile habitat.

text:
Continuous ~ categorical
Regression can represent more types of relationships, such as a continuous response to categorical predictor.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
What’s the “value” of \(x\)?
\[
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x
\]
What is the value of \(x\)? \(\beta_1 \times \text{ENA}\) doesn’t make sense…

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Treat categories as 0’s and 1’s


When area is “ENA”, let \(x=0\)
\[
\begin{align}
y &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 x \\
y &= \beta_0
\end{align}
\]

When area is “ESA”, let \(x=1\)
\[
\begin{align}
y &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 x \\
y &= \beta_0 + \beta_1
\end{align}
\]

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Recode your levels
Conceptually, here’s what happens:


area was a category with two levels.
Pick one level as the reference (“ENA”).
Create a dummy variable for the other level.




This…


# A tibble: 6 × 2
  area  pb_ppm
  <chr>  <dbl>
1 ENA     98.1
2 ENA     54.1
3 ENA    325  
4 ESA    195

…becomes this

    ESA pb_ppm
  <int>  <dbl>

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
New interpretations for \(\beta\)s
With two continuous variables, \(\beta_0\) is the intercept and \(\beta_1\) is the slope.
Look at the statistical notation and the visualization. What do the \(\beta\)s mean now?

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Reference and difference, equation


What is the expected value (\(y\)) when area is “ENA” (\(x=0\))?
\[
\begin{align}
y &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 x \\
y &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 0 \\
y &= \beta_0
\end{align}
\]

What is the expected value (\(y\)) when area is “ESA” (\(x=1\))?
\[
\begin{align}
y &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 x \\
y &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 1 \\
y &= \beta_0 + \beta_1
\end{align}
\]


\(\beta_0\) is now the expected (mean) value of the reference level (ENA here).
\(\beta_1\) is the difference between its level (ESA) and the reference level.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text: Reference and difference, visualized

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Categorical predictors


Linear regression can model the relationship between a continuous response (e.g., soil lead concentrations) and a categorical predictor (e.g., areas ENA and ESA).
One level becomes the reference (e.g., ENA).
The interpretation of the coefficients changes.

\(\beta_0\) becomes the mean of the reference level.
\(\beta_1\) becomes the difference between levels.

The call to lm() is unchanged.

How cool is that??

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Recall multiple regression


\[
\begin{align}
y &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 (x_2=B) + \epsilon \\
\epsilon &\sim Normal(0, \sigma)
\end{align}
\]












Each predictor (\(x_1\), \(x_2=B\)) has it’s own coefficient (\(\beta_1\), \(\beta_2\)). They act on \(y\) separately.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Interactions mediate relationships
In regular multiple regression, the relationship between \(x_1\) and \(y\) is the same regardless of \(x_2\).
But what if the relationship between \(x_1\) and \(y\) varies with \(x_2\)?

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Deforestation and agriculture


Land sparing hypothesis
Increasing yields reduces deforestation.

Rebound hypothesis
Increasing yields incentivizes deforestation.



A section of the Amazon rainforest stands next to soy fields in Belterra, Para state, Brazil, on Nov. 30, 2019. (AP Photo/Leo Correa, File)

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Two hypotheses

What’s the relationship between deforestation and increasing yields?

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Which hypothesis is supported?
Increasing yields increases deforestation: rebound hypothesis

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text: Does the relationship vary?

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Interactive terms
\[
\begin{align}
y &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \beta_3 x_1 x_2 + \epsilon \\
\epsilon &\sim Normal(0, \sigma)
\end{align}
\]
An interaction term multiplies two predictors together

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Deforestation and agriculture model
\[
\begin{align}
\text{Deforestation} &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Yield} + \beta_2 \text{Indig. Steward} \\
&\quad + \beta_3 \text{Yield} \times \text{Indig. Steward} + \epsilon \\
\epsilon &\sim Normal(0, \sigma)
\end{align}
\]
What’s the relationship between deforestion and yield across groups?

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Interactions vary slopes
No indigenous stewardship
\(\text{Indig. Steward} = 0\)
\[
\begin{align}
\text{Deforestation} &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Yield} + \beta_2 \text{Indig. Steward} \\
&\quad + \beta_3 \text{Yield} \times \text{Indig. Steward} \\
\text{Deforestation} &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Yield} + \beta_2 0 + \beta_3 \text{Yield} \times 0 \\
\text{Deforestation} &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Yield}
\end{align}
\]

The slope is \(\beta_1\)

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Interactions vary slopes
Yes indigenous stewardship
\(\text{Indig. Steward} = 1\)
\[
\begin{align}
\text{Deforestation} &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Yield} + \beta_2 \text{Indig. Steward} \\
&\quad + \beta_3 \text{Yield} \times \text{Indig. Steward} \\
\text{Deforestation} &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Yield} + \beta_2 1 + \beta_3 \text{Yield} \times 1 \\
\text{Deforestation} &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Yield} + \beta_2 + \beta_3 \text{Yield} \\
\text{Deforestation} &= \left( \beta_0 + \beta_2 \right) + \left( \beta_1 + \beta_3 \right) \text{Yield}
\end{align}
\]

The slope is \(\beta_1 + \beta_3\)

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text: Interactions vary slopes

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Additive vs. interactive

Additive
\[
\text{Deforestation} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Yield} + \beta_2 \text{Indig. Steward} + \epsilon
\]
Interactive
\[
\begin{align}
\text{Deforestation} &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Yield} + \beta_2 \text{Indig. Steward} \\
&\quad + \beta_3 \text{Yield} \times \text{Indig. Steward} + \epsilon
\end{align}
\]

The only difference is the interaction term, \(\beta_3 \text{Yield} \times \text{Indig. Steward}\)

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Additive model: slope
Yes indigenous stewardship
\(\text{Indig. Steward} = 1\)
\[
\begin{align}
\text{Deforestation} &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Yield} + \beta_2 \text{Indig. Steward} \\
\text{Deforestation} &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Yield} + \beta_2 1 \\
\text{Deforestation} &= \left( \beta_0 + \beta_2 \right) + \beta_1 \text{Yield}
\end{align}
\]

The slope is \(\beta_1\), the same as the no stewardship group. Only the intercept changes.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Interactive model: slope
Yes indigenous stewardship
\(\text{Indig. Steward} = 1\)
\[
\begin{align}
\text{Deforestation} &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Yield} + \beta_2 \text{Indig. Steward} \\
&\quad + \beta_3 \text{Yield} \times \text{Indig. Steward} \\
\text{Deforestation} &= \left( \beta_0 + \beta_2 \right) + \left( \beta_1 + \beta_3 \right) \text{Yield}
\end{align}
\]

The slope is \(\beta_1 + \beta_3\), different from the no stewardship group. Both the intercept and slope change.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Additive vs. interactive


The additive model forces parallel lines. It misses that stewardship removes the rebound effect.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
When to use interactions


Additive
Each predictor affects the response independently.
\(x_2\) shifts \(y\) up or down, but the effect of \(x_1\) on \(y\) is the same.

Interactive
One predictor changes the effect of another on the response.
The effect of \(x_1\) on \(y\) depends on \(x_2\).



Ask: “Does the relationship between \(x_1\) and \(y\) depend on \(x_2\)?”

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Additive is sufficient


Snowpack and elevation
North-facing slopes hold more snow than south-facing slopes at every elevation.
But snowpack increases with elevation at the same rate on both.
Aspect shifts the line; it doesn’t change the slope.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Interactive is necessary


Stream and air temperature
Streams warm as air temperature rises.
But a riparian canopy shades the stream, so shaded streams warm more slowly.
Canopy changes the slope of the relationship.

title: Lab 2: Foundations of Inference
text:
Investigating “yes/no” questions with permutation
Let’s investigate the claim “Lead is elevated in the drip line compared to the rest of the yard” as a yes/no question.

State your hypotheses
Recall that it is more straightforward to find evidence against a hypothesis than for it. So when we investigate yes/no questions, we set up a null hypothesis and see how much evidence there is against it.
State the null and alternative hypotheses for this claim.
\(H_0\): The difference in means is 0.
\(H_A\): The difference in means is greater than 0.


Calculate the observed value of the statistic
We’ll use the difference in means between samples from the drip line and the yard as the statistic for this question.






Important



Remember, the mean isn’t always the most appropriate statistic for representing a distribution! Always think critically about how your data relates to the question.


Calculate the difference in means between the drip line and yard observations in the sample. Remember, this should be a single number (not a data frame or pair of means).

location_summ <- soil_cores |>
  summarize(mean_pb_ppm = mean(pb_ppm), .by = location_code)

obs_diff_means <- location_summ$mean_pb_ppm[2] - location_summ$mean_pb_ppm[1]

obs_diff_means

[1] 172.9459




Shuffle the predictor variable and recalculate the statistic
This statistical experiment simulates the expected variation in our statistic (difference in means) just due to chance alone. To conduct this experiment, we have to break the connection between the predictor variable (location code) and response (lead concentration). Randomizing the predictor leaves the variation in the response untouched, while removing any assocation between the two.
Shuffle the predictor variable and recalculate the statistic. Do it just once - we’ll repeat in the next section.






Tip



sample() can be used to shuffle vectors.



shuffled_summ <- soil_cores |>
  mutate(location_code = sample(location_code)) |>
  summarize(mean_pb_ppm = mean(pb_ppm), .by = location_code)

shuffled_diff_means <- shuffled_summ$mean_pb_ppm[2] -
  shuffled_summ$mean_pb_ppm[1]

shuffled_diff_means

[1] -10.1124




Repeat shuffling
In the previous section, you simulated one statistic from the null hypothesis. What we need now is a whole bunch of statistics from the null hypothesis - our null distribution.
Repeat shuffling 10,000 times to create a vector that simulates the null distribution.






Tip



replicate() repeatedly runs expressions over and over.



location_null_dist <- replicate(
  1e3,
  {
    shuffled_summ <- soil_cores |>
      mutate(location_code = sample(location_code)) |>
      summarize(mean_pb_ppm = mean(pb_ppm), .by = location_code)

    shuffled_summ$mean_pb_ppm[2] -
      shuffled_summ$mean_pb_ppm[1]
  }
)

Visualize the null distribution using a histogram.

tibble(diff_means = location_null_dist) |>
  ggplot(aes(diff_means)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5)














Compare the observed to the null
The previous figure showed the expected distribution of the statistic (the difference in mean lead between drip line and yard) under the null hypothesis. How does that compare to the observed value?
Plot the null distribution again, but this time add a vertical line indicating the observed statistic.

tibble(diff_means = location_null_dist) |>
  ggplot(aes(diff_means)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = obs_diff_means, color = "magenta", linewidth = 1.5)












Calculate your p-value.






Note



A p-value is the probability of observing the sample (or something more extreme) if the null hypothesis is true.



pval <- mean(location_null_dist > obs_diff_means)

pval

[1] 0




Interpret your results
Based on your p-value, do you reject or fail to reject the null hypothesis?
What does this mean for your question?
What characteristics of the data may impact your inference?

title: Lab 2: Foundations of Inference
text:
Investigating “how much?” questions with bootstrapping
Now, let’s investigate the claim “Neighborhoods north of the Exide plant were exposed to more lead than those south” as a how much? question.

Calculate the observed value of the statistic
Once again, let’s use the difference in means as our statistic. Calculate the difference in means between properties in the extended north area and those in the extended south area.






Tip



Use dplyr functions to wrangle the soil core data for this part. Properties starting with “ENA” are in the extended north area, and the “ESA” prefix means extended south area. str_sub() will help here.



ena_esa <- soil_cores |>
  mutate(area = str_sub(property_id, 1, 3)) |>
  filter(area %in% c("ENA", "ESA"))

area_summ <- ena_esa |>
  summarize(mean_pb_ppm = mean(pb_ppm), .by = area) |>
  arrange(area)

obs_diff_means <- area_summ$mean_pb_ppm[1] - area_summ$mean_pb_ppm[2]

obs_diff_means

[1] 72.45974




Resample observations and recalculate the statistic
Bootstrapping simulates the expected variation in our statistic (difference in means) from sampling. Compare this to permutation, which is about variation just due to chance. For this experiment, we will assume the sample is representative of the population and repeatedly draw “new” samples. This process simulates the process of collecting new samples.
Resample rows from the data frame and recalculate the statistic. Repeat this 10,000 times to simulate the sampling distribution.






Tip



Use slice_sample() with replacement to get bootstrap samples.



area_samp_dist <- replicate(
  1e3,
  {
    resampled_summ <- ena_esa |>
      slice_sample(n = nrow(ena_esa), replace = TRUE) |>
      summarize(mean_pb_ppm = mean(pb_ppm), .by = area) |>
      arrange(area)

    resampled_summ$mean_pb_ppm[1] -
      resampled_summ$mean_pb_ppm[2]
  }
)

Visualize the sampling distribution using a histogram.

tibble(diff_means = area_samp_dist) |>
  ggplot(aes(diff_means)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5)














Find the confidence interval
The previous figure showed how your statistic varies due to slight differences between samples. Use this sampling distribution to estimate the 95% confidence interval.






Note



A confidence interval is a range of values that you are confident contains the population parameter.








Tip



Use the quantile() function to find the middle 95% of the sampling distribution.



area_95ci <- quantile(area_samp_dist, c(0.025, 0.975))

Plot the sampling distribution again, but this time add vertical lines indicating the observed statistic and the 95% CI.

tibble(diff_means = area_samp_dist) |>
  ggplot(aes(diff_means)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = obs_diff_means, color = "magenta", linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = area_95ci, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1.5)














Interpret your results
Based on your confidence interval, how much could the difference in lead exposure between north and south be?
What does this mean for your question?
What characteristics of the data may impact your inference?
